gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a named reviewer's measured idle draw with the AC inverter on. That draw runs all night under an RV fridge. The Solar Lab measured about 27 W on the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max and about 17 W on the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. The Gadgeteer measured about 10 W on the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 with AC and DC left on. Separately, Notebookcheck got only about 1,600 Wh out of the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 at a 200 W load (79%), against about 1,850 Wh at 1,800 W.
standout_why: I compared against the cited OutdoorGearLab roundup (updated 2026-07-23). It has measured figures only for the Jackery 2000 v2 (1,710 Wh, 84%) and no idle draw for any product. The cited Popular Mechanics roundup, as ChatGPT quoted it, has usable capacity for the Elite 200 V2 (92%) and no idle draw; I could not open that page myself. Our current Dealectric page cites no named measurements at all. Every ChatGPT runtime table assumes a flat 1,700–1,800 Wh usable and leaves out inverter idle draw. One chat repeats Anker's 'low idle consumption', which is the maker's claim, not a measurement. So rivals cover usable-capacity percentages in part. A side-by-side of measured idle draw, and of capacity at low load (how an RV fridge actually runs), is new.
decides: It confirms the pick rather than changing it. Measured idle draw and low-load capacity count against the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max (27 W idle measured by The Solar Lab) as an overnight RV battery. It is also a caution on the Anker C2000 Gen 2: in Notebookcheck's EU-model test, a 200 W load got only about 79% of rated capacity, so its 9 W idle figure is Anker's own claim. The best measured low-load results belong to the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2: 1.91 kWh discharged (StorageReview) and about 10 W idle with AC and DC on (The Gadgeteer). The top pick, the AC200L, has no independent idle or usable-Wh measurement on the 120 V model. The only figure is BLUETTI's own 12 W self-consumption, quoted by Notebookcheck. So the page can back its runtime claims for the Elite 200 V2 with measurements, but only with maker figures for the AC200L. Illustration, not a measurement: with a 40 W fridge average, 27 W of idle draw makes a 67 W total load against 50 W at 10 W idle. That is about 34% more drain, or roughly 25 h against 34 h from 1,700 Wh.

findings.value: about 40% to 34% over 12 h (about 10 W average, derived)

findings.note: Published 2025-07-07. My arithmetic: 6% of 2,073.6 Wh ≈ 124 Wh, over 12 h ≈ 10 W. The start level is approximate, so this only corroborates The Gadgeteer's figure. Also measured: 0 to 100% on AC in about 1 h 52 min; overload shutoff at 3,300 W.

findings.label: Full discharge and recharge energy (StorageReview)
findings.value: 1.91 kWh discharged (about 92% of 2,073.6 Wh); 2.44 kWh to recharge
findings.source_title: Portable Power Meets Lab-Grade Reliability: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Review (StorageReview, Dylan Dougherty)
findings.note: Published 2025-04-25. Discharge load not stated. The tested unit had 120 V NEMA 5-20 outlets, so it is the North American model. 16 dB 'under small loads'. My arithmetic: round trip 1.91/2.44 ≈ 78%.

findings.label: Self-consumption (BLUETTI's figure, quoted by Notebookcheck; not measured)
findings.value: 12 W; BLUETTI's runtime formula assumes 95% DoD and 93% inverter efficiency (≈1,810 Wh usable)
findings.source_title: Bluetti AC200L hands-on review: Fast-charging power station delivers convincing results (Notebookcheck, Polly Allcock)
findings.note: Published 2024-08-05, updated 2026-02-18. Notebookcheck reviewed the EU/UK/AU model. It quotes BLUETTI's formula ('DoD, η and self-consumption are said to be 95%, 93% and 12W') and says only that the 45-minute runtime at 2,400 W 'roughly tallies' with its testing. My arithmetic: 2,048 × 0.95 × 0.93 ≈ 1,810 Wh. The reviewer confirmed BLUETTI's AC charge times (80% in 45 min, 100% in 1.5 h at 2,400 W).

Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2: no measured idle wattage from any reviewer, and no US-model (120 V) usable-capacity test.

Popular Mechanics' 92% usable-capacity figure for the Elite 200 V2 (quoted in ChatGPT's answer): popularmechanics.com could not be fetched, so I could not confirm the figure, its date or the test method.
